Industry analysts warned that the production cuts could pressure tier-one suppliers and ripple through logistics networks, particularly for semiconductor-intensive components. The company stated it would review production schedules monthly based on market conditions, leaving downstream parts makers exposed to further adjustments if demand fails to recover.

On October 22, 2025, BMW announced that ongoing disruptions at Nexperia, the Dutch chipmaker affected by U.S.-China trade restrictions, will force a temporary reduction in output at its Dingolfing and Regensburg plants starting next week. The automaker cited shortages of essential microcontroller units used in electronic stability and powertrain systems, warning that the suspension of wafer deliveries from Nexperia’s Chinese-linked fabs could last several weeks. Several European automakers, including Volkswagen and Stellantis, reported that their alternative chip sourcing efforts had only partially offset the shortfall, with assembly lines in Germany and Hungary still running at reduced capacity. Volkswagen’s finance chief warned that the prolonged disruption could push the company to accelerate its in-house chip development timeline, potentially moving delivery of its China-focused assisted driving chip forward by a year.

On November 10, 2025, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association urged EU officials to mediate between the Netherlands and China over the Nexperia chip supply disruption, warning that persistent shortages could force additional plant shutdowns within days. Honda, which halted production at its Celaya plant, said it expects to resume operations in early December after receiving export clearance from Chinese authorities. Honda announced an indefinite extension of production halts at its Celaya, Mexico plant and further output cuts at North American facilities, attributing the move to persistent chip shortages from the Dutch-controlled Nexperia. Ford announced a temporary halt at two North American assembly plants due to persistent chip shortages from Nexperia, despite the recent case-by-case export permits. Ford is expected to announce a strategic partnership with a semiconductor manufacturer to secure a stable chip supply for its North American plants, aiming to mitigate the impact of tariffs and the Nexperia chip shortage. A German automaker announced on December 2 that it would temporarily cut production at two domestic plants by 15% through early 2026, citing persistent shortages of application-specific chips previously sourced through Nexperia’s Dutch subsidiary. Ford announced it will indefinitely pause F-150 Lightning production until the aluminum supply recovers, now expected no earlier than Q3 2026, while accelerating development of the Gen 2 model. Separately, Volkswagen and BMW disclosed new supply agreements with U.S. and South Korean chipmakers as part of their push to reduce Chinese dependency, though full diversification remains years away. The broader auto sector faces mounting pressure from semiconductor shortages, aluminum constraints, and shifting consumer demand away from higher-priced EVs.

Following Volkswagen’s €160 billion investment plan, the German automaker announced the closure of its Audi plant in Brussels by February 2026, citing high production costs and weak demand for electric models. Ford CEO Jim Farley announced on December 15 that the automaker would invest $1.2 billion to build a dedicated semiconductor fabrication facility in Ohio, aiming to secure critical chip supply for electric and gas vehicles by 2028. The plant, a joint venture with a U.S.-based chip designer, will focus on mature-node chips used in powertrains and infotainment systems. The announcement follows warnings from the JPMorgan Security and Resilience Initiative advisory council about overreliance on Chinese rare earths and semiconductors. China’s Ministry of Commerce responded that new license applications would be reviewed on a case-by-case basis, emphasizing fair trade principles. Ford executives reiterated calls for sustained U.S.-China cooperation on critical minerals but acknowledged that geopolitical tensions could still disrupt access. The two automakers’ moves highlight a growing divide in supply-chain resilience, with Ford leveraging early diplomatic outcomes while Honda accelerates supplier diversification to avoid future production stoppages.

Honda Motor announced on January 28, 2026, that it has secured a preliminary agreement with Renesas Electronics to increase supply of automotive-grade microcontrollers, but warned that full production recovery will take months.
